title: The Middle Class: Canary in the Gold Mine
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Chuck's birthday, then examine the American middle class: how it is defined (historically, by income, by self-identification, by education and values), its origins from late medieval European burghers and the bourgeoisie, the American Jeffersonian farmer ideal, the nineteenth-century rise of the middle class values system, and its postwar peak fueled by the New Deal, unions, and home ownership. They cover the decline from the mid-1970s (oil crisis, globalization, automation, deunionization, Reagan-era policies, the Clinton-era repeal of Glass-Steagall, the 2008 crisis), wage stagnation versus productivity growth, wealth concentration among the top one percent and the Forbes 400, housing costs, and possible remedies such as expanded social safety nets and free childcare. A listener mail correction about Meharry Medical College closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and Chuck's birthday
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Chuck turning fifty-five, AARP mail, and cheap coffee perks of age.

segments.title: Why the middle class matters and how hard it is to define
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the middle class as a thumbnail metric for societal health and debate whether it is in decline. They note that defining it is difficult and that self-identification matters, referencing Kyla Scanlon and the idea of a vibe session versus a true recession.
topics: middle class as economic health indicator

segments.title: Origins: bourgeoisie and the first middle class
segments.summary: The middle class traces to late medieval Europe, with merchants and bankers of fortified cities (the bourgeoisie) filling the space between peasants and aristocracy. Values shifted from wealth and power to thrift and taste.

segments.title: American experiment, Marx, and middle class values
segments.summary: Jefferson's vision of a nation of self-sufficient yeoman farmers did not materialize as wealthy landowners and then industrialists took power. Marx framed society as owners versus workers. Capitalists needed trained staff, which helped the middle class emerge, and nineteenth-century middle class values stressed hard work, saving, voting rights, education, and the moral role of women in the home.

segments.title: Postwar middle class boom
segments.summary: The middle class grew into the largest group in the US in the twentieth century, powered by the New Deal, the postwar position of the US, government spending from World War II, and union membership. Median real weekly incomes rose between 1940 and 1960, and the Great Compression narrowed wealth gaps. Home ownership also rose after the war.

segments.title: Decline from the 1970s
segments.summary: The hosts describe the end of the postwar boom in the mid-1970s due to European and Japanese competition, the OPEC oil crisis, and social and political conflicts. Manufacturing jobs fell sharply, automation and imports spread, union membership dropped below ten percent, and Reagan-era tax and labor policies favored the wealthy. They also discuss the 2008 crisis and the Clinton-era repeal of Glass-Steagall.

segments.title: Measuring the middle class: income, self-identification, education, values
segments.summary: Pew's income-based definition (two-thirds to double median household income) shows the middle class shrinking from 61 percent of households in 1971 to 51 percent in 2023, with upper and lower shares growing. Gallup 2024 self-identification found 39 percent middle class. The hosts argue education levels are a misleading measure, and values such as economic security, a car per child, family vacations, college, and homeownership define the class.
topics: Pew Research middle class income definition

segments.title: Wages, productivity, and wealth concentration
segments.summary: Average hourly wages for non-supervisory workers peaked around 1973 in inflation-adjusted terms and rose only about $1.50 by 2025, while productivity rose 87 percent from 1979 to 2025 against 33 percent hourly compensation growth. Top one percent wages grew far faster than bottom ninety percent wages. The Forbes 400 had thirteen billionaires in 1982 and now there are more than nine hundred billionaires, and the bottom fifty percent of US wealth holds about four trillion dollars. Richard Reeves' view on zoning and tax policy is cited.

segments.title: Housing, consumer goods, and cost of living
segments.summary: Goods like clothing and electronics have become cheaper, but housing has not. Median house prices rose from about 300,000 to over 400,000 dollars in today's dollars since 1979. Homeownership among forty-year-olds fell from 69 percent for boomers to 62 percent for Gen X, with rent, childcare, college, and healthcare outpacing earnings.

segments.title: Safety nets, European comparison, and possible fixes
segments.summary: The hosts compare European middle class security, citing universal healthcare and stronger social safety nets, and note how inflation hits lower-income households harder. They mention free childcare programs in New Mexico and proposed programs in New York City as possible steps, and Chuck recalls his own experience working at a gas station as a college student.

segments.title: Listener mail: Meharry Medical College correction
segments.summary: A listener from Nashville corrects an earlier episode that placed Meharry Medical College in Georgia; it is in Nashville, Tennessee, founded 1876. The hosts apologize.
